question: In a febrile patient returning from a forested or scrub-vegetated area, actively searching for an eschar (painless, black necrotic skin lesion) in hair-bearing and intertriginous areas is a critical step in the physical examination because its presence is pathognomonic of scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) and directly indicates treatment with doxycycline.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The statement is true. The eschar — a painless black necrotic lesion at the mite bite site — when found, is pathognomonic of scrub typhus. Treatment is doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days. Missing this bedside finding is one of the most preventable diagnostic errors in tropical medicine.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The eschar of scrub typhus is found in <50% of cases even when specifically looked for; missing it in a compatible exposure history means a treatable, potentially fatal rickettsial infection is missed.
